title: Super Washing Machines
description:
# Super Washing Machines

You have `n` super washing machines in one line. `machines[i]` is the number of dresses currently in the `i`th machine.

In one move, you may choose any number of machines. Each chosen machine sends exactly one dress to one adjacent machine at the same time. A machine may receive dresses from its neighbors during the same move.

Return the minimum number of moves needed to make every machine contain the same number of dresses. If the total number of dresses cannot be split evenly across all machines, return `-1`.

## Example 1:

**Input:** machines = [1,0,5]
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** One optimal schedule moves dresses left from the last machine over three rounds until every machine has two dresses.

## Example 2:

**Input:** machines = [0,3,0]
**Output:** 2

## Example 3:

**Input:** machines = [0,2,0]
**Output:** -1
**Explanation:** Two dresses cannot be divided evenly across three machines.

## Constraints:

* `n == machines.length`
* `1 <= n <= 10000`
* `0 <= machines[i] <= 100000`

solutions.name: Running Balance Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

First check whether the total number of dresses is divisible by the number of machines. Then scan from left to right. For each machine, add `machines[i] - target` to a running balance that represents the net number of dresses that must cross the boundary after this machine.

## Key Insight

The answer must be at least the largest absolute boundary flow, because only one dress can cross a fixed boundary per move. It must also be at least the largest positive local surplus, because one machine can send out only one dress per move. The maximum of these two lower bounds is also achievable.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Prefix Boundary Flow
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compare the actual prefix dress count with the prefix count that would exist if every machine already had `target` dresses. Their difference is the signed number of dresses that must cross the boundary after the current machine.

## Key Insight

Every boundary is an independent bottleneck: if a prefix is short by `k`, then `k` dresses must enter from the right across that boundary; if it has `k` extra, then `k` dresses must leave to the right. The answer is the maximum boundary bottleneck and machine surplus bottleneck.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Left and Right Demand Split
solutions.description:
## Approach

For each machine, compute how many dresses the left side still needs and how many the right side still needs. If both sides need dresses, the current machine must send to both sides over different moves; otherwise the larger absolute cross-side flow dominates.

## Key Insight

This view explains the case where one overfull machine must serve both directions. A receiver can accept dresses from both neighbors in one move, but a sender still emits at most one dress per move, so two-sided outgoing demand adds at that machine.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Explicit Boundary Transfer Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build an array where `transfer[i]` is the signed number of dresses that must cross from the left side of boundary `i` to the right side. After computing all boundary transfers, combine their maximum absolute value with the largest local surplus.

## Key Insight

The transfer array turns the greedy invariant into a concrete flow model. Large values in `transfer` are bottlenecks across edges, while large positive `machines[i] - target` values are bottlenecks at senders.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Binary Search on Feasible Move Count
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same bottlenecks as a monotonic feasibility test. A candidate move count `moves` is feasible only if no sender has surplus greater than `moves` and no boundary needs more than `moves` dresses to cross it. Binary search the smallest feasible value.

## Key Insight

Although the optimal answer can be read directly, the feasibility formulation is useful for teaching why the two lower bounds are sufficient. Once a move count covers every sender and every boundary, the schedule can be arranged without a stronger bottleneck.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log S), where `S` is the total number of dresses
- Space Complexity: O(1)
